passage:
Dear Diary,
Monsoon holidays, day 4. Raining AGAIN so no cricket outside.

Watched the old match videos with Ritu didi. I showed her the century by Sameer Khanna, the one where he hit six sixes. Best batsman in the world.

Then she found the match where he got out for zero. I said the umpire was blind. It was clearly not out! Another one, out for 3. I said wet pitch, bad luck.

She said, "Vikas, when your favourite scores, it's talent, and when he doesn't, it's luck?"

I said YES. Because it is.

But now I'm writing this and thinking... maybe I only watch the centuries. I have like 20 saved. I have zero saved of him getting out.

Still best in the world though. Probably.

qa.q: How many century videos does Vikas have saved?
qa.a: Vikas has like 20 saved.

qa.q: Why does Vikas feel so sure the zero was the umpire's fault?
qa.a: Vikas feels loyal and a bit defensive about the favourite batsman, so blaming the umpire feels fair and protects the belief that he is the best.

qa.q: What could Vikas try to test the belief fairly?
qa.a: Vikas could watch a few whole series, good and bad innings, and count them, instead of saving only the centuries.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi see this rainy-day argument?
qa.a: Ritu didi probably finds it funny and a little frustrating, and wants Vikas to notice he only remembers the good matches.

grounding: A child insists a favourite batsman is the best, keeps only the great innings and blames bad scores on the umpire or luck.

The paddy had just been cut in Mohit's village and the whole family sat on the threshing ground in the cold Pongal sun, listening to the match on Thatha's radio.

"Karan Rao will score a hundred," Mohit announced. "He always does."

His cousin Seema, peeling sugarcane, laughed. "Always? He got out for nine last week."

"The ball swung. Nobody could play that ball."

"And the week before? Fourteen."

"Wrong decision. Everyone saw." Mohit's ears went hot.

On the radio, Karan Rao edged the second ball to slip. Out for two.

"That was a no-ball! It must be!"

Seema handed him a piece of sugarcane. "Mohit, you remember his hundreds like festival days. The bad days you forget."

He sat down, chewing hard, and didn't answer.

qa.q: How many runs did Karan Rao score on the radio?
qa.a: Karan Rao was out for two.

qa.q: Why did Mohit's ears go hot when Seema listed low scores?
qa.a: Mohit felt embarrassed and defensive, because the low scores challenged his belief that his favourite always scores.

qa.q: What could Mohit do if he really wants to know how good Karan Rao is?
qa.a: Mohit could write down every score this season, including the low ones, and look at them together.

qa.q: What is it like for Seema to watch Mohit's reaction?
qa.a: Seema seems amused and fond, teasing gently with sugarcane rather than arguing harder.

grounding: A child during the harvest festival explains away his favourite batsman's low scores as bad luck or a wrong decision.

It was the week of Lunar New Year in Sydney, and Xin's grandmother had covered the flat in red paper. He was on the balcony with a radio, listening to the Test.

"Mitchell Hale is the greatest," he told Nkechi. "He never fails."

"He got a duck in Perth," Nkechi said.

"That was a terrible pitch."

"And twelve in Brisbane."

"The umpire. Everyone knows that umpire hates him."

"So when he's good, it's him, and when he's bad, it's everyone else?"

Xin opened his mouth, then shut it. He thought of the scrapbook under his bed, full of cuttings of Hale's big innings. There wasn't a single cutting of the Perth duck. He had torn that page out himself.

"He's still the greatest," Xin muttered, but quieter.

qa.a: Xin's grandmother had covered the flat in red paper.

qa.a: Xin felt uneasy and a little caught out, realising he had torn out the Perth duck and kept only the big innings.

I'm Gargi. In Class 10 I decided Salma was fake. It was one moment: she hugged the new girl on the first day like they were old friends, and something in me said, show-off.

After that, everything was evidence. If Salma laughed at a teacher's joke, she was sucking up. If she posted a quote about kindness, she was performing. The class group kept showing her posts at the top, and I read every one looking for the catch.

What I didn't read: the time she stayed back to help me with chemistry. I told myself it didn't count, she wanted to look good.

It was Salma's mum's illness that cracked it. Salma was quiet for weeks, no posts at all, and still came to help me with chemistry. Nobody was watching. I felt small.

I'd been collecting proof for a story I'd already written.

qa.q: What did Salma do on the first day that made Gargi decide she was fake?
qa.a: She hugged the new girl on the first day like they were old friends.

qa.q: Why did Gargi feel small when Salma kept helping with chemistry?
qa.a: Gargi felt ashamed, because Salma helped even when nobody was watching, which broke the story Gargi had built about her faking kindness.

qa.q: What could Gargi do next time a first impression hardens like this?
qa.a: Gargi could deliberately look for moments that don't fit the story, like the chemistry help, and count them as evidence too.

qa.q: How might Salma have experienced Gargi during those months?
qa.a: Salma may have sensed coldness from Gargi without knowing why, and still chose to help, which probably felt lonely.

grounding: A teenager who has decided a classmate is fake reads everything as proof and dismisses her kind acts.

Class teacher's note, 9B

Nilesh came to see me after the class trip. He wanted to report that Ronit had been "making fun of him behind his back" in the group chat. He had screenshots ready: three messages where Ronit wrote "lol" after Nilesh's posts.

I asked to see the whole chat on his phone. He hesitated, then scrolled. In between the three were many messages he had not screenshotted: Ronit saving him a seat on the bus, Ronit saying "Nilesh's photo is the best one", Ronit asking if he was okay when he felt sick.

He said, "Those are just him pretending." When I asked how he could tell the difference, he couldn't answer.

I didn't argue. I asked him to write two lists: things that fit his idea and things that don't. He sat for ten minutes. The second list was longer.

I'll speak to both boys separately next week.

Payal, class teacher

qa.q: How many messages were in Nilesh's screenshots?
qa.a: Nilesh had screenshots of three messages where Ronit wrote "lol".

qa.q: Why was Nilesh so sure Ronit was mocking him?
qa.a: Nilesh felt hurt and suspicious, so the three "lol" messages seemed to prove it while the kind messages felt like pretending.

qa.q: Why was Payal's two-list idea a good countermeasure?
qa.a: It made Nilesh look at all the evidence himself instead of only the messages that fit, and the longer second list spoke for itself.

qa.q: How might Ronit feel if he learned about the screenshots?
qa.a: Ronit would probably feel surprised and hurt, since he had saved a seat and checked on Nilesh when he was sick.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager who screenshotted only the messages that fit his belief that a classmate mocks him.

By the time the placement cell opened registrations, Seema had already decided to skip them. She wanted a year to prepare for the civil services exam, and she had, she said, done her research.

Her research was a folder on her laptop. Lalremsiami looked through it one evening in their hostel room. An article titled "Why Placements Are a Trap". A video of a topper who said he never took a job. Screenshots of two seniors saying, "Best decision of my life."

"Did you talk to anyone who regretted it?" Lalremsiami asked.

"Why would I? I know what I want."

"What about Arvind bhaiya? He tried for three years and then came back for placements."

Seema's jaw tightened. "His case is different."

She closed the laptop. She felt thoroughly prepared, like someone who had read everything. Lalremsiami noticed the folder had nothing in it that disagreed.

qa.q: What was the article in Seema's folder titled?
qa.a: "Why Placements Are a Trap".

qa.q: Why does Seema feel so well prepared about her decision?
qa.a: Seema feels confident and a bit defensive, because her folder is full of agreeing voices, so it feels like complete research even though nothing in it disagrees.

qa.q: What could Seema add to her research to make it honest?
qa.a: Seema could talk to Arvind bhaiya and others who regretted skipping placements, and read at least one strong case for taking a job first.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see Seema's folder?
qa.a: Lalremsiami sees that the folder only holds agreement, and seems worried Seema is mistaking one-sided reading for research.

I'm Raghav, and last year I nearly talked myself into skipping campus placements to join a friend's music startup.

I thought I was careful. I bookmarked every article about founders who dropped out. I messaged the two seniors who'd started companies and asked them, "Was it worth it?" Of course they said yes; they were the ones it worked for.

My cousin Manjula asked, "Did you look up the ones who didn't make it?" I told her they probably didn't try hard enough. I didn't even notice how quickly I'd said that.

Then one night I actually searched for the other side. A long post by someone whose startup folded, who'd skipped placements and spent two years catching up. It wasn't dramatic. It was just honest.

I still sat for placements. I'm helping the startup on weekends. My folder of bookmarks, I realised, had been a mirror, not a map.

In the polytechnic girls' hostel at Karad, Disha shared a room with Pallavi, who had a plan: delivering fresh buffalo milk by app across the whole district.

Every time someone raised a doubt, Pallavi had an answer ready. The dairy owner said the roads flood in monsoon. "Temporary." A lecturer asked about refrigerated vans. "We'll figure it out." But when a cousin on the phone said, "Great idea!", Pallavi repeated it at dinner for three days.

Disha tried arguing once, point by point: the vans, the roads, the cost. Pallavi only dug in harder, and they didn't speak till morning.

So the next week Disha tried something else. "Can I tell you something I've noticed, not about the idea, about you?" Pallavi nodded, her face wary. "You quote every yes. You wave away every no. That scares me a bit, because I want this to work."

Pallavi was quiet. Then: "Okay. Which no should I take seriously?"

qa.q: What was Pallavi's plan?
qa.a: Delivering fresh buffalo milk by app across the whole district.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when trying the second approach?
qa.a: Disha felt worried for Pallavi and a bit nervous about the reaction, but cared enough to name the pattern gently.

qa.q: Why did naming the pattern work better than arguing point by point?
qa.a: Arguing made Pallavi defend each point, while kindly describing the pattern let her look at how she was listening, without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Disha admitted being scared?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt surprised and a little exposed, but also cared for, which is why she asked which doubt to take seriously.

In their shared flat in Dublin, Hana had watched Emeka's startup idea grow all autumn: a subscription box of Nigerian snacks for students across Europe.

She'd heard every conversation. When his lecturer said shipping costs could sink it, Emeka said the lecturer "didn't get food". When a supplier warned about customs delays, Emeka called him negative. But one comment on a post, "I'd buy this in a heartbeat!", was now printed out and stuck above his desk.

Hana had argued twice. Both times he got louder and she got tired.

One evening, over jollof he'd cooked, she said, "Emeka, I'm not going to argue about shipping. Can I just say what I see? Every yes goes on your wall. Every no goes in the bin."

He put his fork down. He looked at the printout. "That's... fair," he said slowly. "Which no hurts the most?"

"Customs," she said. "Start there."

On Nour's first week at the architecture firm in Amman, she spelled a client's name wrong in an email. Omar, who'd been there two years, noticed. Weak, he thought.

After that, he kept noticing. She arrived four minutes late on Tuesday. She asked where the printer paper was. She paused before answering a question in the review. Each one landed in the same mental file.

What didn't land: that her site drawings were cleaner than his. That the senior partner used her staircase sketch in the final pitch. That she'd stayed back to help the intern with a model. Omar saw all of it, and somehow it slid off.

At the monthly review, the partner asked for opinions on the new hires. Omar opened his mouth to say "not really up to it", and then saw Nour's staircase pinned on the wall behind the partner's head.

He paused. He couldn't remember a single real mistake since that email.

qa.q: What did Nour spell wrong in her first week?
qa.a: Nour spelled a client's name wrong in an email.

qa.q: Why did Omar's first impression feel so reliable to him?
qa.a: Omar felt certain after the email mistake, and each small slip seemed to confirm it, which made him feel observant rather than biased.

qa.q: What could Omar do before giving his opinion at reviews?
qa.a: Omar could list concrete work from the whole period, good and bad, like the staircase sketch and site drawings, before judging.

qa.q: How might Nour experience working with Omar if he never noticed his bias?
qa.a: Nour might feel quietly judged and unsupported despite doing strong work, and could lose confidence or be unfairly passed over.

grounding: A young professional decides early that a new colleague is weak and reads small slips as proof while ignoring her good work.

On day one Vidya labelled a sample tube in the wrong colour. Zainab corrected it and thought, careless.

For the next three weeks, Zainab kept a mental list. Vidya asked a question about the centrifuge. Vidya took a long lunch once. Vidya forgot to restock gloves.

She didn't keep a list of the other things. Vidya caught a mislabelled sample from another ward before it went out. Vidya calmed a frightened child for a blood draw in two minutes when nobody else could.

You asked how I made the call on the new clinic software. Okay, Jaya, so here's what happened. I'm Deepika, I run the front desk at the dental clinic, and I was sure the new system was the answer.

But I've been wrong before when I was sure. So before telling the doctors, I did three things.

First, I asked myself: what would make me say no? I wrote it on a sticky note. If it doubles check-in time. If patients' records can't move over cleanly.

Second, I called our old receptionist, Mrs Fernandes, who hates computers and is very clever. I asked her to find every problem. She found two I'd missed.

Third, I read the most negative reviews of the software.

In the end I still recommended it, but with a slow switch and a backup plan. Her criticism wasn't an attack. It was the best help I got.

qa.a: Deepika felt grateful rather than attacked, seeing the criticism as the best help Deepika got.

qa.a: It fixed the test in advance, so Deepika couldn't quietly move the goalposts once she was attached to the idea.

qa.q: How might the doctors have reacted if Deepika had skipped these steps?

I sit next to Rajni in the planning office. I'm Rashmi. I can only say what I saw.

Rajni had been pushing for weeks to move our school's sports day to a Saturday. She was convinced. Most of us were.

But on Monday she did something I hadn't seen before. She wrote on the whiteboard: "What would change my mind?" Under it: parents who can't come on Saturdays, teachers' weekend duty.

Then she walked over to Mr Joshi, who'd argued against it loudest in the staff meeting. She said, "Give me your best case against. I'm listening." He talked for twenty minutes. She took notes and didn't interrupt once.

On Wednesday she changed her proposal: Saturday, but only for the senior classes, and a weekday option for the juniors. She looked calm, not defeated. When someone asked if she minded losing the argument, she laughed. "I didn't lose. I learned."

qa.q: What did Rajni write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: "What would change my mind?"

qa.q: What did Rashmi seem to feel watching Rajni listen to Mr Joshi?
qa.a: Rashmi seemed surprised and impressed, noting it was something not seen before and that Rajni didn't interrupt once.

qa.q: What did Rajni's approach do well?
qa.a: Rajni set a clear test in advance and invited the strongest critic, which led to a better, blended proposal.

qa.q: How might Mr Joshi have felt being asked for his best case against?
qa.a: Mr Joshi probably felt respected and heard, since his disagreement was treated as useful rather than as an insult.

grounding: A colleague watches a worker invite her strongest critic and name what would change her mind before committing.

Christmas week in Bandra, and the lane outside St Peter's was strung with paper stars. Jaya had saved forty rupees for the sticker stall that Deepika, a Class 7 girl, ran from a shoebox.

"The glitter unicorn is thirty," Deepika said.

Thirty! Jaya's heart sank.

"Twenty-five?" Jaya tried.

"Okay, twenty-five, since it's Christmas."

Jaya skipped home, feeling clever. She'd saved five whole rupees!

At home her brother looked at the sticker. "They sell those at the stationery shop for ten."

It had felt like such a good deal. Twenty-five was so much less than thirty. But it was still more than twice what it cost at the shop.

She stuck it in her notebook anyway. But next time, she decided, she'd check the shop first.

qa.q: How much did the stationery shop sell the sticker for?
qa.a: They sell those at the stationery shop for ten.

qa.q: Why did Jaya feel so clever after paying twenty-five?
